units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So, Ben. After all that, what is Brussels now?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On paper, the Brussels-Capital Region.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Nineteen municipalities, about one and a quarter million people.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Grand Place?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Is in the City of Brussels. Which is only one of those nineteen.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So when someone says Brussels, they could mean three different things.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At least three.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The other eighteen have their own mayors and councils, don't they?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And names that Brusselers use as proudly as the name of the city itself.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ixelles, Saint-Gilles, Schaerbeek, Anderlecht, Molenbeek, Uccle, and more.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The region is the capital of Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's the capital of the Flemish Community and of the French Community.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And, informally but unmistakably, the capital of Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Four capitals in one. That's a lot of hats.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And one very small head.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, but the governance. Explain it to me like I'm five.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Belgium is a federation of three regions and three language communities, layered on top of each other.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels sits where they all overlap.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The regional parliament has a French-speaking group and a Dutch-speaking group, and the government has to include members of both.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which sounds like a clever safeguard.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. It also makes things slow.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Very slow, recently.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After regional elections in June of 2024, the parties couldn't agree on a coalition.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It took 613 days. More than twenty months.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Six hundred and thirteen days.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A seven-party government finally took office in February of 2026, led by a French-speaking liberal, Boris Dilliès.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The parties had to promise to balance a budget that was deeply in deficit, and to merge various regional agencies.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So for almost two years, the capital of Europe ran on a caretaker government.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It did.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Stubbornness tally. I think we have to.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Twenty months without a government, and the trams still ran?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I'd say seven.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Seven. And that's just the region.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the national level, the story was similar.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After elections in June of 2024, it took more than two hundred thirty days to form a federal government.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In February of 2025, Bart De Wever was sworn in as prime minister by King Philippe, in a five-party coalition.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And De Wever is a Flemish nationalist.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Who had long dreamed of a more independent Flanders.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The first Flemish nationalist to lead the Belgian government.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Running the country he'd like to split.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The kind of irony Belgian history delivers on a regular basis.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the king?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philippe, who succeeded his father Albert the Second in 2013.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The seventh king of the Belgians.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Governments come and go.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who actually lives here?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the first of January, 2025, the region counted about one million, two hundred fifty-six thousand people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A bit over thirty-seven percent of them held a foreign passport.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that doesn't count the Belgians with a foreign background.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: No. Residents come from about a hundred and eighty-three different nationalities.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A hundred and eighty-three. There are only a hundred and ninety-some countries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So almost the whole world is represented in one very small region.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who are the biggest groups?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The largest foreign group is French.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then Romanians and Italians, then Spaniards and Moroccans.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels also has an important Congolese community, centered on a district called Matongé.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I read something surprising about the population.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2025, for the first time since the mid-nineteen-nineties, it stopped growing.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And a lot of those foreign residents work for the institutions.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The European Commission, the Council of the European Union, and parts of the European Parliament all have their seats here, around the Schuman roundabout and the Rue de la Loi.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: NATO's headquarters, a striking new complex in the north of the city, opened in 2018.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How many people work for international institutions?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the most recent count, more than fifty thousand in the region.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Around them are embassies, trade associations, law firms, think tanks, and the lobbyists who try to influence the laws of the European Union.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So a city that once lived by cloth and tapestries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now lives largely by words and rules.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which is still a kind of weaving, if you think about it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With a lot more meetings.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It hasn't all been easy, though.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The city has had dark days.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It has. In November of 2015, after the terror attacks in Paris, some of whose planners had lived in the Brussels district of Molenbeek, the city went into a security lockdown that lasted days.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Soldiers on the streets, the metro closed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then, in March.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the eighteenth of March, 2016, police captured one of the key suspects, Salah Abdeslam, in Molenbeek.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Four days later, on the morning of the twenty-second, three suicide bombers struck.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Where?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Two bombs exploded in the departure hall of Brussels Airport at Zaventem.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: An hour later, a third went off on a metro train leaving Maalbeek station, in the heart of the European Quarter, among the offices of the institutions.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How many people were killed?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Thirty-two people, not counting the attackers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More than three hundred were injured.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Islamic State group claimed responsibility.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the city remembers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every year since, the city has marked the anniversary.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the little statue of the Manneken Pis has been dressed in a firefighter's uniform to honor the rescuers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And yet life goes on, and the city keeps reinventing itself.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It does. In 2015, the central boulevards around the Bourse were closed to cars, creating one of the largest pedestrian zones in Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The old Boulevard Anspach, built over the buried Senne, became a place to walk and sit.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The river we buried.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now with a sidewalk café on top.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the rest of the city?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A low-emission zone limits older cars.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a traffic plan called Good Move, which reduces through traffic in residential neighborhoods, has been bitterly debated.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Like most such efforts.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels is trying to become a city for people rather than just for commuters.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And, like most such efforts, it's argued over fiercely.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Let's turn to the fun. Because the culture is as eclectic as the population.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels is the capital of the comic strip.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There are dozens of giant murals of comic heroes painted on building walls across the city, a museum devoted to the art form, and a tradition that gave the world Tintin and the Smurfs.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, I would like to do a comic-strip wall walk right now.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It exists. You can.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And beer and chocolate.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2016, UNESCO recognized Belgian beer culture as part of the world's cultural heritage.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And according to tradition, the praline, the filled chocolate, was invented in 1912 by a Brussels chocolatier named Jean Neuhaus, in the elegant glass-roofed Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the oldest covered shopping arcades in Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Waffles. Fries. Mussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a small green vegetable that carries the city's name.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Brussels sprout.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Which was grown in the area around the city centuries ago.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The vegetable everyone loves to hate, named after the city that loves everything.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I'd say that's unfair to the sprout.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Fair. Now, the city is also reckoning with its past.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. The Royal Museum for Central Africa, in Tervuren, which Leopold the Second built as a showcase of his colony, was closed for years.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It reopened in 2018 after a major renovation that tried to confront its colonial origins.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the statues.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2020, during worldwide protests against racism, statues of Leopold the Second in Belgium were defaced, and some were removed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there was a royal apology.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A parliamentary commission examined Belgium's colonial past.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 2022, King Philippe visited the Democratic Republic of the Congo and expressed deep regret for the suffering caused by colonial rule.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The debate is ongoing, and it will shape how the city understands itself in the years ahead.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. If you had to pick one symbol for Brussels, what would it be?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not a lion, or a saint, or a king.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A dog.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A dog. In the local dialect, a zinneke is a mongrel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A mixed-breed street dog that belongs to no one breed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brusselers say it with affection.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For their city. A place of mixed languages, mixed origins, and mixed styles, where no one is quite purebred.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There's a small bronze statue of a dog, relieving itself against a post, on a street in the old center.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a colorful parade, held every two years, that celebrates the zinneke spirit.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A dog that is also, let's be honest, a bit rude.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A very Brussels dog.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: All right. Let's step back and look at the whole journey.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It began as a settlement in a marsh, with a chapel on an island.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It became a market town on the road between Flanders and Cologne, and a ducal capital.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its guilds won a seat at the table.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It became the capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands, the home of great painters and weavers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was nearly erased in 1695, and rebuilt in four years into one of the most beautiful squares in the world.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It passed from Spain to Austria to France to the Dutch.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1830, after a night at the opera and four days of street fighting, it became the capital of a new nation.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It grew rich under Leopold, on the profits of an empire built on terrible cruelty.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was occupied twice, and spared the worst of two world wars.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And then, almost by accident, it became the working capital of a united Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Through all of it, Brussels has been a place where different peoples and languages meet, argue, trade, and build together.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It has never had one identity.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And perhaps that is its identity.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Which brings us to the final stubbornness tally.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Final count. Eight.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Eight. For a city that survived fire, bombardment, two occupations, and a government that took twenty months to form.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And somehow still serves excellent fries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That is the story of Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Thank you for listening.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And enjoy the city.
